expectedText:
BREACH OF FIDUCIARY DUTY BETWEEN SPOUSES (FAMILY CODE SECTION 1101 REMEDIES) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Morgan Casey Lee

PARTY STATEMENT
I, Jordan Alex Lee, state that I am or was married to Morgan Casey Lee, that the marriage took place on June 14, 2015, and that I have read this information sheet, which describes the California statutes and published case law governing a claim by one spouse against the other for breach of the fiduciary duty that spouses owe each other with respect to community property, and the remedies a court may award for such a breach under Family Code section 1101. This document is informational only. It does not itself assert, establish, or waive any claim, and it is not a pleading, a demand, or a court order -- only a court, applying the statutes and case law described in this document to evidence presented to it, can determine whether a breach of fiduciary duty has occurred and what remedy follows.

SCOPE: THE SECTION 1101 CLAIM AND ITS REMEDIES, NOT THE DISCLOSURE FORMS OR OMITTED-ASSET PROCEDURE
This document addresses the statutory claim one spouse holds against the other for breach of the interspousal fiduciary duty as it affects community property, and the remedies Family Code section 1101 attaches to that claim: an accounting, reformation of title, a mandatory award of 50 percent of an undisclosed or transferred asset plus attorney's fees and costs, and a mandatory award of 100 percent of the asset where the breach involves oppression, fraud, or malice. It does not address the separate mandatory financial-disclosure procedure in a dissolution, legal separation, or nullity proceeding (the preliminary and final declarations of disclosure under Family Code sections 2100 through 2113 and the sanctions for noncompliance under section 2107), the post-judgment procedure for dividing a community asset that a judgment omitted or failed to adjudicate (Family Code section 2556), or the reimbursement and charging rules for post-separation payments and post-separation use of community assets (Watts charges and Epstein credits) -- each of which this project covers in a separate information sheet. The general statement of the interspousal fiduciary duty in Family Code section 721(b) also appears, in a drafting context, in this project's Postnuptial Agreement; this document restates it only as the foundation for the section 1101 claim.

THE INTERSPOUSAL FIDUCIARY DUTY THAT A SECTION 1101 CLAIM ENFORCES
Under California law, either spouse may enter into any transaction with the other, or with any other person, respecting property, which either might enter into if unmarried -- but transactions between spouses are subject to the general rules governing fiduciary relationships that control the actions of persons occupying confidential relations with each other. That confidential relationship imposes on each spouse a duty of the highest good faith and fair dealing, and neither spouse may take any unfair advantage of the other. It is this statutory duty, together with the management-and-control duty described in the next clause, whose breach gives rise to the claim and remedies described in the rest of this document.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "Subject to subdivision (b), either spouse may enter into any transaction with the other, or with any other person, respecting property, which either might if unmarried."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 721(a) (California Legislative Information text), spouses' freedom to transact, subject to the fiduciary rules of subdivision (b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=721.)
  "in transactions between themselves, spouses are subject to the general rules governing fiduciary relationships that control the actions of persons occupying confidential relations with each other. This confidential relationship imposes a duty of the highest good faith and fair dealing on each spouse, and neither shall take any unfair advantage of the other."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 721(b) (California Legislative Information text), the interspousal fiduciary duty of the highest good faith and fair dealing (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=721.)
  Known gap: This is a single California statute (Fam. Code § 721), used as real evidence of the source of the interspousal fiduciary duty that § 1101 enforces -- not a claim about the law of any other state. Both quotations are from the same section and are not independent of each other. The statute's cross-references to specified Probate Code sections (excepting certain transactions) and to Corporations Code sections 16403, 16404, and 16503 (nonmarital business partners' rights and duties, including access to books, rendering true and full information on request, and accounting for and holding as trustee any benefit derived from a nonconsensual transaction) are not quoted here; the Postnuptial Agreement's fiduciary-duty clause in this project quotes the full text of § 721(b) including those enumerated duties.

THE FIDUCIARY DUTY IN MANAGING COMMUNITY ASSETS: FULL DISCLOSURE, EQUAL ACCESS, AND RESTRICTIONS ON GIFTS
In the management and control of community assets and liabilities, each spouse is required by statute to act toward the other in accordance with the general rules governing fiduciary relationships, as specified in Family Code section 721, until the assets and liabilities have been divided by the parties or by a court. This duty includes the obligation to make full disclosure to the other spouse of all material facts and information regarding the existence, characterization, and valuation of all assets in which the community has or may have an interest and all debts for which the community is or may be liable, and to provide equal access, upon request, to all information, records, and books that pertain to the value and character of those assets and debts. The same statute also provides that a spouse may not make a gift of community personal property, or dispose of community personal property for less than fair and reasonable value, without the other spouse's written consent -- a restriction that does not apply to gifts mutually given by both spouses to third parties or to gifts from one spouse to the other. Where a spouse who has primary management and control of a community business fails to give the other spouse the prior written notice the statute requires before disposing of all or substantially all of the business's personal property, the statute states that the remedies for that failure are only those specified in section 1101.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "Each spouse shall act with respect to the other spouse in the management and control of the community assets and liabilities in accordance with the general rules governing fiduciary relationships which control the actions of persons having relationships of personal confidence as specified in Section 721, until such time as the assets and liabilities have been divided by the parties or by a court. This duty includes the obligation to make full disclosure to the other spouse of all material facts and information regarding the existence, characterization, and valuation of all assets in which the community has or may have an interest and debts for which the community is or may be liable, and to provide equal access to all information, records, and books that pertain to the value and character of those assets and debts, upon request."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 1100(e) (California Legislative Information text), the fiduciary duty in management and control, full disclosure, and equal access until division (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=1100.)
  "A spouse may not make a gift of community personal property, or dispose of community personal property for less than fair and reasonable value, without the written consent of the other spouse. This subdivision does not apply to gifts mutually given by both spouses to third parties and to gifts given by one spouse to the other spouse."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 1100(b) (California Legislative Information text), restriction on gifts and below-value dispositions of community personal property (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=1100.)
  "Remedies for the failure by a managing spouse to give prior written notice as required by this subdivision are only as specified in Section 1101. A failure to give prior written notice shall not adversely affect the validity of a transaction nor of any interest transferred."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 1100(d) (California Legislative Information text), remedies for a managing spouse's failure to give prior written notice are only those in section 1101 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=1100.)
  Known gap: This is a single California statute (Fam. Code § 1100), used as real evidence of the content of the management-and-control fiduciary duty -- not a survey of how courts have applied it, and not a claim about any other state's law. The three quotations are from different subdivisions of the same section and are not independent of one another. This clause does not reproduce § 1100(a) (each spouse's general management-and-control power over community personal property), § 1100(c) (the written-consent requirement for selling, conveying, or encumbering community personal property used as the family dwelling, household furnishings, or the other spouse's or minor children's clothing), or the full text of § 1100(d) (primary management and control of a community business, and the rule that a failure to give prior written notice does not affect the validity of the transaction); management and control of community real property is governed by a separate section (Fam. Code § 1102) that is not addressed here.

THE STATUTORY CLAIM: IMPAIRMENT OF A SPOUSE'S PRESENT UNDIVIDED ONE-HALF INTEREST IN THE COMMUNITY ESTATE
Family Code section 1101 gives a spouse a claim against the other spouse for any breach of the fiduciary duty that results in impairment to the claimant spouse's present undivided one-half interest in the community estate. The claim expressly extends both to a single transaction and to a pattern or series of transactions that have caused, or will cause, a detrimental impact to the claimant spouse's undivided one-half interest. The statute also provides that an action under it may be brought without filing an action for dissolution of marriage, legal separation, or nullity; it may instead be brought in conjunction with such an action, or upon the death of a spouse. A California Court of Appeal has described section 1101 as creating a right of action and specific remedies for the breach of fiduciary duty between spouses.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "A spouse has a claim against the other spouse for any breach of the fiduciary duty that results in impairment to the claimant spouse’s present undivided one-half interest in the community estate, including, but not limited to, a single transaction or a pattern or series of transactions, which transaction or transactions have caused or will cause a detrimental impact to the claimant spouse’s undivided one-half interest in the community estate."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 1101(a) (California Legislative Information text), the claim for breach of fiduciary duty impairing a spouse's one-half community interest (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=1101.)
  "Any action may be brought under this section without filing an action for dissolution of marriage, legal separation, or nullity, or may be brought in conjunction with the action or upon the death of a spouse."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 1101(f) (California Legislative Information text), the action may be brought with or without a dissolution, legal separation, or nullity action (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=1101.)
  "Importantly, section 1101 creates a right of action and specific remedies for the breach of fiduciary duty between spouses."
  — In re Marriage of Margulis, (2011) 198 Cal. App. 4th 1252, 1270 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5810544/prentis-margulis-v-margulis/)
  Known gap: The two statutory quotations are from different subdivisions of the same section (Fam. Code § 1101(a) and (f)) and are not independent of each other; the case-law quotation is a single published Court of Appeal decision characterizing the statute, offered as real evidence of how a California court has described it rather than as an independent source of the statutory text. This clause does not address § 1101(e), under which a court may, on a spouse's motion, dispense with the other spouse's otherwise-required consent to a transaction affecting community property when the transaction is in the best interest of the community and consent has been arbitrarily refused or cannot be obtained because of the nonconsenting spouse's physical or mental incapacity or prolonged absence. What conduct amounts to a breach in a particular case, and what impairment must be shown, are questions decided on the evidence in each case and are not resolved by the statutory text alone.

COURT-ORDERED ACCOUNTING, CLASSIFICATION OF PROPERTY, AND REFORMATION OF TITLE
Among the remedies the statute makes available, a court may order an accounting of the property and obligations of the parties to a marriage, and may determine the rights of ownership in, the beneficial enjoyment of, or access to, community property, as well as the classification of all property of the parties to the marriage. A court may also order that the name of a spouse be added to community property held in the name of the other spouse alone, or that the title of community property held in some other title form be reformed to reflect its community character. The title-reformation remedy is subject to four stated exceptions: a partnership interest held by the other spouse as a general partner; an interest in a professional corporation or professional association; an asset of an unincorporated business if the other spouse is the only spouse involved in operating and managing the business; and any other property, if the revision would adversely affect the rights of a third person.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "A court may order an accounting of the property and obligations of the parties to a marriage and may determine the rights of ownership in, the beneficial enjoyment of, or access to, community property, and the classification of all property of the parties to a marriage."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 1101(b) (California Legislative Information text), court may order an accounting and determine ownership, enjoyment, access, and classification (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=1101.)
  "A court may order that the name of a spouse shall be added to community property held in the name of the other spouse alone or that the title of community property held in some other title form shall be reformed to reflect its community character, except with respect to any of the following: (1) A partnership interest held by the other spouse as a general partner. (2) An interest in a professional corporation or professional association. (3) An asset of an unincorporated business if the other spouse is the only spouse involved in operating and managing the business. (4) Any other property, if the revision would adversely affect the rights of a third person."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 1101(c) (California Legislative Information text), court may add a spouse's name to title or reform title, subject to four exceptions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=1101.)
  Known gap: The two quotations are from adjacent subdivisions of the same statute (Fam. Code § 1101(b) and (c)) and are not independent of each other. This clause states what the statute permits a court to order; it does not describe the procedure for requesting an accounting or title reformation, the showing a court requires before ordering one, or how these remedies interact with the monetary remedies in § 1101(g) and (h) described in the following clauses.

TIME LIMITS: THREE YEARS FROM ACTUAL KNOWLEDGE, THE DISSOLUTION AND DEATH EXCEPTIONS, AND LACHES
An action on the statutory claim generally must be commenced within three years of the date the petitioning spouse had actual knowledge that the transaction or event for which the remedy is sought occurred. That three-year limit does not apply, however, when the action is commenced upon the death of a spouse or in conjunction with an action for legal separation, dissolution of marriage, or nullity; the statute states that such an action may be brought without regard to the three-year limitation. The defense of laches may be raised in any action brought under the section. Except for actions brought in the dissolution, legal separation, nullity, or death contexts, the statutory remedies apply only to transactions or events occurring on or after July 1, 1987.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "(d) (1) Except as provided in paragraph (2), any action under subdivision (a) shall be commenced within three years of the date a petitioning spouse had actual knowledge that the transaction or event for which the remedy is being sought occurred. (2) An action may be commenced under this section upon the death of a spouse or in conjunction with an action for legal separation, dissolution of marriage, or nullity without regard to the time limitations set forth in paragraph (1). (3) The defense of laches may be raised in any action brought under this section. (4) Except as to actions authorized by paragraph (2), remedies under subdivision (a) apply only to transactions or events occurring on or after July 1, 1987."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 1101(d) (California Legislative Information text), three-year limitations period, exceptions, laches, and the July 1, 1987 cutoff (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=1101.)
  Known gap: This is a single statutory subdivision (Fam. Code § 1101(d)), quoted in full, and used as real evidence of the limitations rule -- not a survey of how courts have applied the 'actual knowledge' trigger or the laches defense in particular cases, and not a claim about any other state's limitations period. The statute's reference to 'actual knowledge' is not further defined in the section, and this clause does not attempt to define it.

THE MANDATORY 50 PERCENT REMEDY, VALUATION AT HIGHEST VALUE, AND ATTORNEY'S FEES
For a breach of the fiduciary duty by one spouse, including the duties set out in Family Code sections 721 and 1100, the statute provides that the remedies shall include, but are not limited to, an award to the other spouse of 50 percent, or an amount equal to 50 percent, of any asset undisclosed or transferred in breach of the fiduciary duty, plus attorney's fees and court costs. The statute directs that the value of the asset be determined as its highest value at the date of the breach of the fiduciary duty, the date of the sale or disposition of the asset, or the date of the award by the court. A California Court of Appeal has described this 50 percent award as mandatory, and has noted, citing an earlier decision of the same court, that where a spouse's breach involves conduct not amounting to fraud, oppression, or malice, the accompanying award of attorney's fees under this subdivision is likewise mandatory -- in contrast with the discretionary treatment of fees under the 100 percent remedy described in the next clause.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "Remedies for breach of the fiduciary duty by one spouse, including those set out in Sections 721 and 1100, shall include, but not be limited to, an award to the other spouse of 50 percent, or an amount equal to 50 percent, of any asset undisclosed or transferred in breach of the fiduciary duty plus attorney’s fees and court costs. The value of the asset shall be determined to be its highest value at the date of the breach of the fiduciary duty, the date of the sale or disposition of the asset, or the date of the award by the court."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 1101(g) (California Legislative Information text), the 50 percent remedy, highest-value valuation, and attorney's fees and costs (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=1101.)
  "The statutory remedies for a breach of fiduciary duty, specifically including a breach of “those [duties] set out in Sections 721 and 1100,” include a mandatory award of 50 percent “of any asset undisclosed or transferred in breach of the fiduciary duty plus attorney’s fees and court costs. . . .” (§ 1101, subd. (g).)"
  — In re Marriage of Margulis, (2011) 198 Cal. App. 4th 1252, 1270 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5810544/prentis-margulis-v-margulis/)
  "where breach of fiduciary duty by a spouse involves conduct not amounting to fraud, oppression, or malice within the meaning of Civ. Code, § 3294, an award of fees is mandatory, in contrast with the discretionary fee provision of Fam. Code, § 1101, subd. (h)"
  — In re Marriage of Rossi, (2001) 90 Cal. App. 4th 34, 43 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5808687/rossi-v-rossi/)
  Known gap: The statutory quotation is a single subdivision (Fam. Code § 1101(g)). The two case-law quotations are from two different published Court of Appeal opinions (Margulis and Rossi), but the Rossi passage is itself a bracketed parenthetical summarizing a still-earlier decision (In re Marriage of Hokanson (1998) 68 Cal.App.4th 987), which this document did not independently fetch; the characterization of the § 1101(g) fee award as mandatory therefore rests on Rossi's description of Hokanson rather than on Hokanson's own text. The Rossi opinion, decided in 2001, quoted the then-current version of § 1101(g) in a footnote; that subdivision was amended effective January 1, 2002 (adding the reference to § 1100 and the highest-value valuation sentence, and removing a former sentence about interest), and this clause relies on the current statutory text rather than the version Rossi quoted. The Margulis quotation appears in that opinion's summary of the statutory scheme rather than as its holding.

THE 100 PERCENT REMEDY FOR BREACHES INVOLVING OPPRESSION, FRAUD, OR MALICE
Where a spouse's breach of the fiduciary duty set forth in Family Code sections 721 and 1100 falls within the ambit of Civil Code section 3294 -- California's punitive-damages statute -- the remedies shall include, but are not limited to, an award to the other spouse of 100 percent, or an amount equal to 100 percent, of any asset undisclosed or transferred in breach of the fiduciary duty. Civil Code section 3294 applies where it is proven by clear and convincing evidence that the defendant has been guilty of oppression, fraud, or malice, and it defines each term: 'malice' means conduct intended by the defendant to cause injury to the plaintiff, or despicable conduct carried on with a willful and conscious disregard of the rights or safety of others; 'oppression' means despicable conduct that subjects a person to cruel and unjust hardship in conscious disregard of that person's rights; and 'fraud' means an intentional misrepresentation, deceit, or concealment of a material fact known to the defendant, with the intention of thereby depriving a person of property or legal rights or otherwise causing injury. A California Court of Appeal reviewing a 100 percent award has stated that, because section 3294 requires clear and convincing proof, the appellate inquiry is whether the record contains substantial evidence to support a determination by clear and convincing evidence.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "Remedies for the breach of the fiduciary duty by one spouse, as set forth in Sections 721 and 1100, when the breach falls within the ambit of Section 3294 of the Civil Code shall include, but not be limited to, an award to the other spouse of 100 percent, or an amount equal to 100 percent, of any asset undisclosed or transferred in breach of the fiduciary duty."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 1101(h) (California Legislative Information text), the 100 percent remedy where the breach falls within Civil Code section 3294 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=1101.)
  "In an action for the breach of an obligation not arising from contract, where it is proven by clear and convincing evidence that the defendant has been guilty of oppression, fraud, or malice, the plaintiff, in addition to the actual damages, may recover damages for the sake of example and by way of punishing the defendant."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 3294(a) (California Legislative Information text), the clear-and-convincing standard for oppression, fraud, or malice (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=3294.)
  "(1) “Malice” means conduct which is intended by the defendant to cause injury to the plaintiff or despicable conduct which is carried on by the defendant with a willful and conscious disregard of the rights or safety of others. (2) “Oppression” means despicable conduct that subjects a person to cruel and unjust hardship in conscious disregard of that person’s rights. (3) “Fraud” means an intentional misrepresentation, deceit, or concealment of a material fact known to the defendant with the intention on the part of the defendant of thereby depriving a person of property or legal rights or otherwise causing injury."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 3294(c) (California Legislative Information text), statutory definitions of malice, oppression, and fraud (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=3294.)
  "Because Civil Code section 3294 requires proof by “clear and convincing evidence” of fraud, oppression, or malice, we must inquire whether the record contains “ ‘substantial evidence to support a determination by clear and convincing evidence"
  — In re Marriage of Rossi, (2001) 90 Cal. App. 4th 34, 40 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5808687/rossi-v-rossi/)
  Known gap: The quotations are from two different statutes (Fam. Code § 1101(h) and Civ. Code § 3294(a) and (c)), the second of which is incorporated by reference in the first, plus one published Court of Appeal opinion describing the standard of review; the § 3294 quotations are from the same section and are not independent of each other. Civil Code § 3294 is a general civil-damages statute whose subdivisions (b), (d), and (e) (employer liability for employees' acts, wrongful-death actions following a felony homicide conviction, and a 1988 effective-date provision) are not relevant to the interspousal context and are omitted here. Whether particular conduct meets the § 3294 definitions is a fact question decided on the evidence in each case.

CASE ILLUSTRATION: INTENTIONAL CONCEALMENT OF A COMMUNITY ASSET (IN RE MARRIAGE OF ROSSI)
In In re Marriage of Rossi, a California Court of Appeal affirmed a post-judgment order awarding one former spouse 100 percent of lottery winnings that the other spouse had intentionally concealed during the dissolution proceedings. The concealing spouse had filed for dissolution after learning of the winnings, had consulted lottery personnel about avoiding sharing the prize, had used a relative's address for lottery correspondence, and had omitted the winnings from her disclosure documents and the marital settlement agreement; the trial court rejected her testimony that the prize was a gift and therefore her separate property. The Court of Appeal held that this record supported a finding of fraud within the meaning of Civil Code section 3294 and that the case presented precisely the circumstance section 1101(h) is intended to address. The court found nothing in the statute's language to justify an exception to the 100 percent penalty based on the supposed unclean hands of the spouse from whom the asset was concealed, described the statute as unambiguous with no exception provided, and explained that the strong language of section 1101(h) serves the purpose of ensuring full disclosure of marital assets, which it called absolutely essential to a trial court's determination of property division and support. The court also noted that under section 1101(h) the award of the entire asset is mandatory while an award of attorney's fees is discretionary, and that the trial court acted within its discretion in declining to add a fee award.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "This case presents precisely the circumstance that Family Code section 1101, subdivision (h) is intended to address. Here, one spouse intentionally concealed a significant community property asset."
  — In re Marriage of Rossi, (2001) 90 Cal. App. 4th 34, 42 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5808687/rossi-v-rossi/)
  "The strong language of section 1101, subdivision (h) serves an important purpose: full disclosure of marital assets is absolutely essential to the trial court in determining the proper dissolution of property and resolving support issues."
  — In re Marriage of Rossi, (2001) 90 Cal. App. 4th 34, 42 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5808687/rossi-v-rossi/)
  "We find nothing in the language of the statute to justify an exception to the penalty provision of Family Code section 1101, subdivision (h) because of the supposed unclean hands of the spouse from whom the asset was concealed."
  — In re Marriage of Rossi, (2001) 90 Cal. App. 4th 34, 42 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5808687/rossi-v-rossi/)
  "The statute provides that, where a spouse conceals assets under circumstances satisfying the criteria for punitive damages under Civil Code section 3294, a penalty representing 100 percent of the concealed asset is warranted. The statute is unambiguous and no exception is provided."
  — In re Marriage of Rossi, (2001) 90 Cal. App. 4th 34, 43 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5808687/rossi-v-rossi/)
  "“The clear import of the language in subdivision (h) is that an award of attorney fees is discretionary, over and above the mandatory award of the entire asset at issue.”"
  — In re Marriage of Rossi, (2001) 90 Cal. App. 4th 34, 42 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5808687/rossi-v-rossi/)
  Known gap: This is a single published California Court of Appeal decision, used as real evidence of how a California court has applied Fam. Code § 1101(h) to intentional concealment of a community asset -- not a survey of all published or unpublished authority on the section, and not a prediction of how any other case would be decided; the outcome turned on the trial court's credibility findings, which the appellate court reviewed only for substantial evidence. All quotations are from the same opinion and are not independent of one another. The court's statement that the award of the entire asset is mandatory while fees are discretionary is itself a quotation from the same court's earlier decision in In re Marriage of Hokanson (1998) 68 Cal.App.4th 987, which this document did not independently fetch. The opinion also affirmed on an alternative ground -- breach of the disclosure warranties in the parties' marital settlement agreement -- which this clause does not address.

MISSING ASSETS UNDER A MANAGING SPOUSE'S POST-SEPARATION CONTROL: BURDEN OF PROOF (IN RE MARRIAGE OF MARGULIS)
In In re Marriage of Margulis, a California Court of Appeal addressed who bears the burden of proof when community assets that were under one spouse's control after separation have disappeared by the time of trial. The court held that once a nonmanaging spouse makes a prima facie showing of the existence and value of community assets in the other spouse's control post-separation, the burden of proof shifts to the managing spouse to prove the proper disposition or lesser value of those assets, and that if the managing spouse fails to carry that burden, the court should charge the managing spouse with the assets according to the prima facie showing. The court grounded this rule in general equitable principles governing when the burden of proof shifts (including the parties' unequal access to evidence), in the Family Code provisions that impose fiduciary duties of disclosure and accounting on spouses -- sections 721, 1100, 1101, and 2100 -- and in prior family law decisions addressing missing community assets. The court observed that when one spouse has exclusive control over community property, the parties will have vastly unequal access to evidence concerning its disposition, and that in that situation fairness requires shifting the burden of proof on missing assets to the managing spouse.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "Once a nonmanaging spouse makes a prima facie showing of the existence and value of community assets in the other spouse’s control postseparation, the burden of proof shifts to the managing spouse to prove the proper disposition or lesser value of those assets. Failing such proof, the court should charge the managing spouse with the assets according to the prima facie showing."
  — In re Marriage of Margulis, (2011) 198 Cal. App. 4th 1252, 1258 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5810544/prentis-margulis-v-margulis/)
  "We conclude that once a nonmanaging spouse makes a prima facie showing concerning the existence and value of community assets in the control of the other spouse postseparation, the burden of proof shifts to the managing spouse to rebut the showing or prove the proper disposition or lesser value of these assets. If the managing spouse fails to meet this burden, the court should charge the managing spouse with the assets according to the prima facie showing."
  — In re Marriage of Margulis, (2011) 198 Cal. App. 4th 1252, 1267 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5810544/prentis-margulis-v-margulis/)
  "When this occurs, fairness requires shifting to the managing spouse the burden of proof on missing assets. Moreover, as explained in the next part, the statutory fiduciary duties of disclosure and accounting owed between spouses further justify that result."
  — In re Marriage of Margulis, (2011) 198 Cal. App. 4th 1252, 1268 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5810544/prentis-margulis-v-margulis/)
  Known gap: This is a single published California Court of Appeal decision, used as real evidence of a burden-of-proof rule California courts apply to missing community assets -- not a survey of all authority on the point and not a claim about any other state's law. All quotations are from the same opinion and are not independent of one another; the court itself described the rule as one advocated by amici curiae but not fully articulated in any published case before it. The rule concerns allocation of the burden of proof at trial; it does not itself determine what constitutes a sufficient 'prima facie showing,' which is decided on the evidence in each case, and this clause does not address the opinion's further discussion of the particular evidence in that case, its treatment of the parties' equalizing payment, or its separate holdings on other issues.

expectedJSON.body: I, Jordan Alex Lee, state that I am or was married to Morgan Casey Lee, that the marriage took place on June 14, 2015, and that I have read this information sheet, which describes the California statutes and published case law governing a claim by one spouse against the other for breach of the fiduciary duty that spouses owe each other with respect to community property, and the remedies a court may award for such a breach under Family Code section 1101. This document is informational only. It does not itself assert, establish, or waive any claim, and it is not a pleading, a demand, or a court order -- only a court, applying the statutes and case law described in this document to evidence presented to it, can determine whether a breach of fiduciary duty has occurred and what remedy follows.

This document addresses the statutory claim one spouse holds against the other for breach of the interspousal fiduciary duty as it affects community property, and the remedies Family Code section 1101 attaches to that claim: an accounting, reformation of title, a mandatory award of 50 percent of an undisclosed or transferred asset plus attorney's fees and costs, and a mandatory award of 100 percent of the asset where the breach involves oppression, fraud, or malice. It does not address the separate mandatory financial-disclosure procedure in a dissolution, legal separation, or nullity proceeding (the preliminary and final declarations of disclosure under Family Code sections 2100 through 2113 and the sanctions for noncompliance under section 2107), the post-judgment procedure for dividing a community asset that a judgment omitted or failed to adjudicate (Family Code section 2556), or the reimbursement and charging rules for post-separation payments and post-separation use of community assets (Watts charges and Epstein credits) -- each of which this project covers in a separate information sheet. The general statement of the interspousal fiduciary duty in Family Code section 721(b) also appears, in a drafting context, in this project's Postnuptial Agreement; this document restates it only as the foundation for the section 1101 claim.

Under California law, either spouse may enter into any transaction with the other, or with any other person, respecting property, which either might enter into if unmarried -- but transactions between spouses are subject to the general rules governing fiduciary relationships that control the actions of persons occupying confidential relations with each other. That confidential relationship imposes on each spouse a duty of the highest good faith and fair dealing, and neither spouse may take any unfair advantage of the other. It is this statutory duty, together with the management-and-control duty described in the next clause, whose breach gives rise to the claim and remedies described in the rest of this document.

expectedJSON.body: In the management and control of community assets and liabilities, each spouse is required by statute to act toward the other in accordance with the general rules governing fiduciary relationships, as specified in Family Code section 721, until the assets and liabilities have been divided by the parties or by a court. This duty includes the obligation to make full disclosure to the other spouse of all material facts and information regarding the existence, characterization, and valuation of all assets in which the community has or may have an interest and all debts for which the community is or may be liable, and to provide equal access, upon request, to all information, records, and books that pertain to the value and character of those assets and debts. The same statute also provides that a spouse may not make a gift of community personal property, or dispose of community personal property for less than fair and reasonable value, without the other spouse's written consent -- a restriction that does not apply to gifts mutually given by both spouses to third parties or to gifts from one spouse to the other. Where a spouse who has primary management and control of a community business fails to give the other spouse the prior written notice the statute requires before disposing of all or substantially all of the business's personal property, the statute states that the remedies for that failure are only those specified in section 1101.

expectedJSON.body: Family Code section 1101 gives a spouse a claim against the other spouse for any breach of the fiduciary duty that results in impairment to the claimant spouse's present undivided one-half interest in the community estate. The claim expressly extends both to a single transaction and to a pattern or series of transactions that have caused, or will cause, a detrimental impact to the claimant spouse's undivided one-half interest. The statute also provides that an action under it may be brought without filing an action for dissolution of marriage, legal separation, or nullity; it may instead be brought in conjunction with such an action, or upon the death of a spouse. A California Court of Appeal has described section 1101 as creating a right of action and specific remedies for the breach of fiduciary duty between spouses.

expectedJSON.body: Among the remedies the statute makes available, a court may order an accounting of the property and obligations of the parties to a marriage, and may determine the rights of ownership in, the beneficial enjoyment of, or access to, community property, as well as the classification of all property of the parties to the marriage. A court may also order that the name of a spouse be added to community property held in the name of the other spouse alone, or that the title of community property held in some other title form be reformed to reflect its community character. The title-reformation remedy is subject to four stated exceptions: a partnership interest held by the other spouse as a general partner; an interest in a professional corporation or professional association; an asset of an unincorporated business if the other spouse is the only spouse involved in operating and managing the business; and any other property, if the revision would adversely affect the rights of a third person.

expectedJSON.body: For a breach of the fiduciary duty by one spouse, including the duties set out in Family Code sections 721 and 1100, the statute provides that the remedies shall include, but are not limited to, an award to the other spouse of 50 percent, or an amount equal to 50 percent, of any asset undisclosed or transferred in breach of the fiduciary duty, plus attorney's fees and court costs. The statute directs that the value of the asset be determined as its highest value at the date of the breach of the fiduciary duty, the date of the sale or disposition of the asset, or the date of the award by the court. expectedJSON.body: Where a spouse's breach of the fiduciary duty set forth in Family Code sections 721 and 1100 falls within the ambit of Civil Code section 3294 -- California's punitive-damages statute -- the remedies shall include, but are not limited to, an award to the other spouse of 100 percent, or an amount equal to 100 percent, of any asset undisclosed or transferred in breach of the fiduciary duty. Civil Code section 3294 applies where it is proven by clear and convincing evidence that the defendant has been guilty of oppression, fraud, or malice, and it defines each term: 'malice' means conduct intended by the defendant to cause injury to the plaintiff, or despicable conduct carried on with a willful and conscious disregard of the rights or safety of others; 'oppression' means despicable conduct that subjects a person to cruel and unjust hardship in conscious disregard of that person's rights; and 'fraud' means an intentional misrepresentation, deceit, or concealment of a material fact known to the defendant, with the intention of thereby depriving a person of property or legal rights or otherwise causing injury. A California Court of Appeal reviewing a 100 percent award has stated that, because section 3294 requires clear and convincing proof, the appellate inquiry is whether the record contains substantial evidence to support a determination by clear and convincing evidence.

expectedJSON.body: In In re Marriage of Rossi, a California Court of Appeal affirmed a post-judgment order awarding one former spouse 100 percent of lottery winnings that the other spouse had intentionally concealed during the dissolution proceedings. The concealing spouse had filed for dissolution after learning of the winnings, had consulted lottery personnel about avoiding sharing the prize, had used a relative's address for lottery correspondence, and had omitted the winnings from her disclosure documents and the marital settlement agreement; the trial court rejected her testimony that the prize was a gift and therefore her separate property. The Court of Appeal held that this record supported a finding of fraud within the meaning of Civil Code section 3294 and that the case presented precisely the circumstance section 1101(h) is intended to address. The court found nothing in the statute's language to justify an exception to the 100 percent penalty based on the supposed unclean hands of the spouse from whom the asset was concealed, described the statute as unambiguous with no exception provided, and explained that the strong language of section 1101(h) serves the purpose of ensuring full disclosure of marital assets, which it called absolutely essential to a trial court's determination of property division and support. The court also noted that under section 1101(h) the award of the entire asset is mandatory while an award of attorney's fees is discretionary, and that the trial court acted within its discretion in declining to add a fee award.

expectedJSON.body: In In re Marriage of Margulis, a California Court of Appeal addressed who bears the burden of proof when community assets that were under one spouse's control after separation have disappeared by the time of trial. The court held that once a nonmanaging spouse makes a prima facie showing of the existence and value of community assets in the other spouse's control post-separation, the burden of proof shifts to the managing spouse to prove the proper disposition or lesser value of those assets, and that if the managing spouse fails to carry that burden, the court should charge the managing spouse with the assets according to the prima facie showing. The court grounded this rule in general equitable principles governing when the burden of proof shifts (including the parties' unequal access to evidence), in the Family Code provisions that impose fiduciary duties of disclosure and accounting on spouses -- sections 721, 1100, 1101, and 2100 -- and in prior family law decisions addressing missing community assets. The court observed that when one spouse has exclusive control over community property, the parties will have vastly unequal access to evidence concerning its disposition, and that in that situation fairness requires shifting the burden of proof on missing assets to the managing spouse.
